Pulmonology · published research

Pleurisy

A 2003 controlled report described faster pleural-effusion resorption and symptom relief with laser added to usual care. A 2004 rehabilitation report described improved lung function and diaphragm mobility but combined laser with breathing exercises, so the laser effect cannot be isolated.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 2003 controlled report described faster pleural-effusion resorption and symptom relief with laser added to usual care. A 2004 rehabilitation report described improved lung function and diaphragm mobility but combined laser with breathing exercises, so the laser effect cannot be isolated.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Respiratory system > Pleurisy category contains three animal experiments. Two additional human reports are narrowly mapped from adjacent clinical literature, bringing the relevant set to five titles. Both human papers are from the same Serbian research group and center; cohort overlap is unclear, so their patient totals should not be assumed independent.

Human and clinical evidence

Milojević and Kuruc's 2003 prospective controlled report compared 25 patients receiving laser biostimulation plus usual care with 25 controls. It described faster pleural-effusion resorption, symptom remission, and lower inflammatory markers, but did not report random allocation (DOI 10.2298/MPNS0312516M, Article). A 2004 report involving 175 patients combined laser biostimulation with breathing exercises and conventional care and described improved lung-function measures and diaphragm mobility. Because the intervention was combined, the laser contribution cannot be separated (PubMed).

Animal evidence

Three carrageenan-induced pleurisy experiments in mice and rats report changes in leukocyte migration or inflammatory measures. They are preclinical results, not patient evidence (Lopes-Martins et al. 2005 Lopes-Martins et al. 2006 Boschi et al. 2008).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or ex-vivo study is listed for this indication.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human reports used laser biostimulation at acupuncture and local points, with repeated sessions over approximately ten days in the 2003 report. The animal studies used red light in induced inflammatory models. Wavelength indicates the light's color band and affects tissue penetration, but reporting is incomplete across the small mapped human reports.

Interpretation

The human reports suggest possible short-term changes in specific pleurisy settings, but allocation, co-interventions, and possible cohort overlap limit attribution. Animal findings provide separate mechanistic evidence. Independent randomized studies are needed to assess symptom relief and effusion recovery.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term symptom and effusion outcomes in two controlled Serbian reports Very low for attributing benefit to laser alone because one report added breathing exercises and cohort overlap is unclear
Publications and records5 relevant titles (3 exact animal studies plus 2 mapped Serbian human reports)

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two human reports describe symptom, effusion, or lung-function changes, but neither establishes randomized laser effects. The larger report combined laser with breathing exercises, and the same authors worked at the same center. Prospective randomized studies should isolate PBM and use predefined recovery outcomes.
